headline: Trade finance offers a $2.5 trillion funding gap opportunity with structural tailwinds from supply chain security, energy security, trade recalibration and energy transition
reasoning: Kazaur Rahman explains that the Asian Development Bank has identified a USD 2.5 trillion trade finance funding gap that is set to grow, creating a significant opportunity for non-bank lenders. Banks dominate the space but cannot expand infinitely due to capital constraints, so they rotate capital to institutional asset managers who co-invest alongside them. Structural macro themes — supply chain security, energy security, trade recalibration and energy transition — can all be captured through trade finance allocations. In a higher-for-longer rate environment, the asset class generates defensive, realised income via amortising, self-liquidating loans backed by contractual cash flows.
quote: I think the opportunities there's a very good opportunity set given that you know, the market itself, there is a trade finance funding gap that's been that number of two and a half, 2 1/2 trillion U.S. dollars. That's been the Asian Development Bank have done their research and that's the that's the number that they put the gap to be that's going to increase. So there is an opportunity set where if you invest in this space, you can help bridge that funding gap. But then also at the same time, you can capture these structural tailwinds which are happening in the world from, you know, from supply chain security, energy security, you know, trade recalibration, energy transition. By investing in this trade finance asset class, you can capture these structural trends going on in the world too.

headline: Concentration risk — not trade finance per se — caused Baffler-style blow-ups; properly diversified trade finance portfolios with counterparty limits avoid that dynamic
reasoning: Rahman draws a sharp distinction between the Baffler situation, where multiple loans to different projects ultimately concentrated performance risk on a single developer, and a well-constructed trade finance portfolio where concentration limits are actively monitored. He argues that because trade finance loans are amortising and self-liquidating, as long as the manager avoids concentrated positions and enforces counterparty limits, the portfolio generates consistent, defensive cash flows rather than being exposed to a single point of failure. The comparison is used to reassure investors that trade finance does not carry the same structural liquidity and concentration risks that surfaced in Baffler.
quote: The way it's very different from Baffler is that, you know, Baffler, you're effectively, you have all these individual loans to different projects, but if you take a step back, you're really taking concentration risk on the same developer. So you take performance risk on the same developer. So when that developer falls away, everything starts to unravel. Whilst in this asset class, you know you, if you do it right, where you, you know, you don't take concentrated positions when you invest in a loan and you make sure you monitor your different, your counterparty concentration limits. You can construct an incredibly diversified portfolio where you know, they're all the loans are amortising and it's, it's, you know, it's generating consistent cash flows. So consistent cash flows from interest payments, from principal amortisation payments. So you really are generating defensive realised income. It's a very different risk profile from Baffler.

headline: Self-liquidating, amortising structure makes trade finance more defensive than traditional bullet-loan private credit, avoiding refinancing risk and offering consistent realised income
reasoning: Rahman contrasts trade finance loans — which are purpose-specific, amortising and repaid directly from the cash flows of the underlying trade or project activity — with traditional private credit loans, which are bullet in nature and carry refinancing risk tied to LTV covenants, valuation multiples or asset sales. Because trade finance loans are backed by the production and sale of essential goods, investors are repaid from contractual cash flows rather than relying on a refinancing event. The asset class also offers substantial diversification across borrower types (financial institutions, corporates, sovereigns, project finance) and loan structures (receivables, working capital, term loans), making it possible to construct a portfolio generating consistent income from both interest and principal amortisation.
quote: What makes them very different from say traditional private credit is that the loans are specifically, specifically being used to finance some form of trade activity or project activity. They're being used by the borrower to finance the OpEx, the working capital, the cap, the CapEx and that from those processes it then uses, it uses a loan proceeds to then produce an essential good and then it sells that essential good to say an international multinational off taker. So the key difference between traditional private credit is that with these loans, they're, they're amortising loans, they're self liquidating with typically backed by contractual cash flows and you're getting repaid directly from the cash flows generated from the trade activity or the project project activity. Whilst when you look at traditional private credit, typically those loans are bullet loans and they're being used to either finance leverage or being used to finance a sponsor dividend recap. And because they're bullet in nature, there's always a refi risk around them.
